title: AdaPreLoRA: Adafactor Preconditioned Low-Rank Adaptation

paper.title: AdaPreLoRA: Adafactor Preconditioned Low-Rank Adaptation
paper.abstract: Abstract Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reparameterizes a weight update as a product of two low-rank factors, but the Jacobian J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}} of the generator mapping the factors to the weight matrix is rank-deficient, so the factor-space preconditioner J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ℱ t ​ J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}\mathcal{F}_{t}J_{\mathcal{G}} induced by any 𝑾 \bm{W} -space preconditioner ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} is singular, and consequently the standard chain rule cannot be uniquely inverted to map a preconditioned 𝑾 \bm{W} -space direction back to a factor-space update. We cast existing LoRA optimizers in a unified framework parameterized by two choices: (i) which invertible surrogate for J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ℱ t ​ J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}\mathcal{F}_{t}J_{\mathcal{G}} to use, and (ii) which ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} on 𝑾 \bm{W} to use. Existing methods occupy four families along these axes: factor-space adaptive updates, block-diagonal surrogates for J 𝒢 ∗ ​ J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}J_{\mathcal{G}} , Frobenius-residual pseudoinverse methods, and Riemannian manifold constraint. Within this design space, a gradient-statistics-aware ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} paired with a closed-form factor-space solve at 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) \mathcal{O}((m+n)r) memory remains underexplored. We propose AdaPreLoRA , which fills this gap by adopting the Adafactor diagonal Kronecker preconditioner ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} on 𝑾 \bm{W} and selecting from the resulting factor-space solution family the element minimizing an ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} -weighted imbalance between the two factor contributions; by construction, the resulting factor update is the closest LoRA approximation to the preconditioned 𝑾 \bm{W} -space direction under the ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} -weighted norm. Across GPT-2 (E2E), Mistral-7B and Qwen2-7B (GLUE, ARC, GSM8K), and diffusion-model personalization, AdaPreLoRA is competitive with or improves over a representative set of LoRA optimizers while keeping peak GPU memory at the LoRA optimizer level.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Fine-tuning large pretrained models [ 18 , 35 , 2 ] for downstream tasks is increasingly bottlenecked by the cost of full-parameter updates, motivating parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 14 ] has become the standard PEFT method: it freezes the pretrained weight 𝑾 0 \bm{W}_{0} and reparameterizes its update as a product 𝑩 ​ 𝑨 \bm{B}\bm{A} with 𝑩 ∈ ℝ m × r \bm{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} , 𝑨 ∈ ℝ r × n \bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} , r ≪ min ⁡ ( m , n ) r\ll\min(m,n) , reducing trainable parameters and optimizer state from 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ n ) \mathcal{O}(mn) to 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) \mathcal{O}((m+n)r) . A growing line of work [ 11 , 37 , 32 , 39 , 40 , 33 , 21 , 38 ] extends this template with refined optimizers in pursuit of full-fine-tuning quality at LoRA’s memory budget. Despite this progress, optimizing in the factor space [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] [\bm{B},\bm{A}] rather than directly in 𝑾 \bm{W} raises a fundamental obstruction (§ 2 ): writing 𝒢 : [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] ↦ 𝑩 ​ 𝑨 \mathcal{G}:[\bm{B},\bm{A}]\mapsto\bm{B}\bm{A} for the map generating the factors to the weight matrix, its Jacobian J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}} is rank-deficient because 𝒢 \mathcal{G} has a built-in redundancy under the gauge reparameterization ( 𝑩 , 𝑨 ) ↦ ( 𝑩 ​ 𝑪 , 𝑪 − 1 ​ 𝑨 ) (\bm{B},\bm{A})\mapsto(\bm{B}\bm{C},\bm{C}^{-1}\bm{A}) for any invertible 𝑪 \bm{C} . Since practical gradient-statistical preconditioners are typically approximations to the Fisher information in the parameter space being optimized, the relevant preconditioner in factor space is the Fisher information with respect to [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] [\bm{B},\bm{A}] . By the chain rule, this operator must take the form J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ℱ t ​ J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}\mathcal{F}_{t}J_{\mathcal{G}} , where ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} is the corresponding gradient-statistical preconditioner in 𝑾 \bm{W} -space. Because J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ℱ t ​ J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}\mathcal{F}_{t}J_{\mathcal{G}} is singular, it cannot be uniquely inverted to map a 𝑾 \bm{W} -space preconditioned direction back to a factor-space update. Existing LoRA optimizers respond to this obstruction along several directions. Cheap factor-space schemes preserve the 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) \mathcal{O}((m+n)r) memory budget but discard the gradient-statistics structure on 𝑾 \bm{W} , either by sidestepping the framework altogether (vanilla LoRA [ 14 ] and Imbalance-Reg [ 40 ] , which apply per-coordinate adaptive updates directly on the factors) or by taking ℱ t = 𝑰 \mathcal{F}_{t}=\bm{I} with block-diagonal approximations of ( J 𝒢 ∗ ​ J 𝒢 ) (J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}J_{\mathcal{G}}) (LoRA+ [ 11 ] , Riemannian Preconditioned LoRA [ 37 ] ). LoRA-Pro [ 33 ] stays in the affine solution set of ( 7 ) by minimizing the Frobenius residual ‖ J 𝒢 ​ [ 𝚫 𝑩 t , 𝚫 𝑨 t ] − ℱ t − 1 ​ 𝑮 t ‖ F 2 \|J_{\mathcal{G}}[\bm{\Delta}_{\bm{B}_{t}},\bm{\Delta}_{\bm{A}_{t}}]-\mathcal{F}_{t}^{-1}\bm{G}_{t}\|_{F}^{2} ; its AdamW variant pairs a non-trivial ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} on 𝑾 \bm{W} with a Frobenius (rather than ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} -weighted) residual, mismatching the preconditioner’s metric, and explicitly maintains 𝑾 \bm{W} -space first/second moments at 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ n ) \mathcal{O}(mn) memory prohibitive at LLM scale. Manifold-based methods (Riemannian Muon [ 5 ] , RAdamW [ 4 ] ) take a Riemannian gradient step on ℳ r \mathcal{M}_{r} in the ambient 𝑾 \bm{W} -space and rely on a retraction back to the manifold, rather than a closed-form solution of ( 7 ) in factor coordinates. A gradient-statistics-aware J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ℱ t ​ J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}\mathcal{F}_{t}J_{\mathcal{G}} paired with 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) \mathcal{O}((m+n)r) memory in the LoRA factor space remains an underexplored design point. We target this point by observing that, even though J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ℱ t ​ J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}\mathcal{F}_{t}J_{\mathcal{G}} is singular, the linear system J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ℱ t ​ J 𝒢 ​ [ 𝑷 , 𝑸 ] = J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ( 𝑮 t ) J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}\mathcal{F}_{t}J_{\mathcal{G}}\,[\bm{P},\bm{Q}]=J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}(\bm{G}_{t}) on the factor pair [ 𝑷 , 𝑸 ] [\bm{P},\bm{Q}] is always consistent: its solution set is a non-empty r 2 r^{2} -dimensional affine subspace, the directions in factor space whose induced 𝑾 \bm{W} -update equals ℱ t − 1 ​ 𝑮 t \mathcal{F}_{t}^{-1}\bm{G}_{t} projected onto 𝕋 t = range ⁡ ( J 𝒢 ) \mathbb{T}_{t}=\mathrm{range}(J_{\mathcal{G}}) , the subspace of 𝑾 \bm{W} -changes a single LoRA step can express. Designing a LoRA optimizer in this framework therefore decomposes into two coupled choices (§ 3 ): (i) which gradient-statistics-aware preconditioner ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} to use on 𝑾 \bm{W} , and (ii) how to select a particular element of the affine solution set. For (i), we adopt the Adafactor [ 28 ] diagonal Kronecker form ℱ t = 𝑳 t ⊗ 𝑹 t \mathcal{F}_{t}=\bm{L}_{t}\otimes\bm{R}_{t} (with operator square root ℋ t = ℱ t 1 / 2 \mathcal{H}_{t}=\mathcal{F}_{t}^{1/2} , acting as ℋ t ​ 𝒀 = 𝑳 t 1 / 2 ​ 𝒀 ​ 𝑹 t 1 / 2 \mathcal{H}_{t}\bm{Y}=\bm{L}_{t}^{1/2}\bm{Y}\bm{R}_{t}^{1/2} ), the cheapest non-trivial 𝑾 \bm{W} -space preconditioner ( 𝒪 ⁡ ( m + n ) \mathcal{O}(m+n) memory). For (ii), we use the fact that all elements of the affine solution set induce the same 𝑾 \bm{W} -update (the ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} -orthogonal projection of ℋ t − 1 ​ 𝑮 t \mathcal{H}_{t}^{-1}\bm{G}_{t} onto 𝕋 t \mathbb{T}_{t} ) but trace different factor trajectories, and pick the element that minimizes the ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} -norm imbalance ‖ 𝚫 𝑩 t ​ 𝑨 t − 𝑩 t ​ 𝚫 𝑨 t ‖ ℋ t 2 \|\bm{\Delta}_{\bm{B}_{t}}\bm{A}_{t}-\bm{B}_{t}\bm{\Delta}_{\bm{A}_{t}}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{t}}^{2} between the two factor contributions to the 𝑾 \bm{W} -update. The resulting algorithm, Ada factor Pre conditioned Lo w- R ank A daptation ( AdaPreLoRA ), admits a closed-form factor update at 𝒪 ⁡ ( r 3 ) \mathcal{O}(r^{3}) extra cost and keeps the optimizer state at 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) \mathcal{O}((m+n)r) . By construction, its 𝑾 \bm{W} -update is the closest point in 𝕋 t \mathbb{T}_{t} to the Adafactor-preconditioned direction ℋ t − 1 ​ 𝑮 t \mathcal{H}_{t}^{-1}\bm{G}_{t} under the ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} -weighted norm. Cheap factor-space schemes lack this guarantee, since their updates do not arise as a 𝑾 \bm{W} -space preconditioned direction projected onto 𝕋 t \mathbb{T}_{t} . Empirically (§ 4 ), AdaPreLoRA matches or outperforms vanilla LoRA, Scaled AdamW, LoRA-Pro AdamW, and SOAP across GPT-2 (E2E), Mistral-7B and Qwen2-7B (GLUE, ARC, GSM8K), and diffusion-model fine-tuning, while matching Scaled AdamW’s peak memory and avoiding the ∼ 2 × \sim 2\times memory overhead of LoRA-Pro AdamW. Our contributions are: • A unified framework that recasts existing LoRA optimizers as instances of the consistent linear system J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ℱ t ​ J 𝒢 ​ [ 𝚫 𝑩 t , 𝚫 𝑨 t ] = J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ( 𝑮 t ) J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}\mathcal{F}_{t}J_{\mathcal{G}}\,[\bm{\Delta}_{\bm{B}_{t}},\bm{\Delta}_{\bm{A}_{t}}]=J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}(\bm{G}_{t}) , parameterized by the choice of preconditioner ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} and the rule that selects an element of the affine solution set (§ 2.2 ). • AdaPreLoRA , a LoRA optimizer whose 𝑾 \bm{W} -update is the closest point in 𝕋 t \mathbb{T}_{t} to the Adafactor-preconditioned direction ℋ t − 1 ​ 𝑮 t \mathcal{H}_{t}^{-1}\bm{G}_{t} under the ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} -weighted norm, recovered in closed form at 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) \mathcal{O}((m+n)r) memory (§ 3 ). • Experimental evidence that the resulting update direction is competitive with or improves over both cheap factor-space and pseudoinverse-based baselines, including at the 7B parameter scale.

sections.heading: 2.3 Choosing ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} : Adaptive Preconditioner Toolkit on 𝑾 \bm{W}
sections.text: The gap identified above asks for an ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} that is gradient-statistics-based yet cheap on 𝑾 \bm{W} . We review the standard families of 𝑾 \bm{W} -space preconditioners, organized by memory cost. All families construct a second-moment-based preconditioner ℱ t : ℝ m × n → ℝ m × n \mathcal{F}_{t}:\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} from gradient outer-product statistics of the form 𝑮 t ​ 𝑮 t ⊤ \bm{G}_{t}\bm{G}_{t}^{\top} or 𝑮 t ⊙ 𝑮 t \bm{G}_{t}\odot\bm{G}_{t} , and produce the preconditioned update 𝑾 t + 1 = 𝑾 t − η t ​ ℱ t − 1 ​ 𝑮 t \bm{W}_{t+1}=\bm{W}_{t}-\eta_{t}\mathcal{F}_{t}^{-1}\bm{G}_{t} ; they differ in the structure imposed on ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} , which trades off expressiveness against cost. AdaGrad [ 8 ] and Adam [ 16 ] approximate ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} by its diagonal 𝒉 t ∈ ℝ m ​ n \bm{h}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{mn} as an exponential moving average of 𝑮 t ⊙ 𝑮 t \bm{G}_{t}\odot\bm{G}_{t} , yielding per-coordinate rescaling that ignores the matrix structure of 𝑮 t \bm{G}_{t} at memory 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ n ) \mathcal{O}(mn) . Adafactor [ 28 ] compresses this further into a rank-1 Kronecker form by maintaining only the row sums 𝒍 t ∈ ℝ m \bm{l}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and column sums 𝒓 t ∈ ℝ n \bm{r}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} of 𝑮 t ⊙ 𝑮 t \bm{G}_{t}\odot\bm{G}_{t} (the elementwise Hadamard product), dropping the memory cost to 𝒪 ⁡ ( m + n ) \mathcal{O}(m+n) . Shampoo [ 10 ] maintains 𝑳 Sh , t = 𝑳 Sh , t − 1 + 𝑮 t ​ 𝑮 t ⊤ ∈ ℝ m × m \bm{L}_{{\rm Sh},t}=\bm{L}_{{\rm Sh},t-1}+\bm{G}_{t}\bm{G}_{t}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} and 𝑹 Sh , t = 𝑹 Sh , t − 1 + 𝑮 t ⊤ ​ 𝑮 t ∈ ℝ n × n \bm{R}_{{\rm Sh},t}=\bm{R}_{{\rm Sh},t-1}+\bm{G}_{t}^{\top}\bm{G}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} and updates by 𝑾 t + 1 = 𝑾 t − 𝑳 Sh , t − 1 4 ​ 𝑮 t ​ 𝑹 Sh , t − 1 4 \bm{W}_{t+1}=\bm{W}_{t}-\bm{L}_{{\rm Sh},t}^{-\frac{1}{4}}\bm{G}_{t}\bm{R}_{{\rm Sh},t}^{-\frac{1}{4}} ; SOAP [ 22 , 30 ] runs Adam in the eigenbasis of the Shampoo preconditioner; and K-FAC [ 20 , 19 ] factorizes ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} as the Kronecker product of activation and gradient covariances. All three impose 𝒪 ⁡ ( m 2 + n 2 ) \mathcal{O}(m^{2}+n^{2}) memory and 𝒪 ⁡ ( m 3 + n 3 ) \mathcal{O}(m^{3}+n^{3}) per-step inverse cost, which dominates LoRA’s budgets. Among these candidates, the Adafactor diagonal Kronecker form ℱ t = 𝑳 t ⊗ 𝑹 t \mathcal{F}_{t}=\bm{L}_{t}\otimes\bm{R}_{t} is the only one that is simultaneously gradient-statistics-based and cheap ( 𝒪 ⁡ ( m + n ) \mathcal{O}(m+n) memory). Our method (§ 3 ) adopts this candidate and pairs it with a closed-form solution of the linear system ( 7 ) that respects the LoRA factorization.

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Results
sections.text: We evaluate AdaPreLoRA against representatives of the design families identified in Table 1 : vanilla LoRA / AdamW (identity replacement), Scaled GD / Scaled AdamW (Riemannian Preconditioned LoRA [ 37 ] with SGD / AdamW; block-diagonal J 𝒢 ∗ ​ J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}J_{\mathcal{G}} ), LoRA-Pro SGD / AdamW [ 33 ] (Moore–Penrose J 𝒢 † J_{\mathcal{G}}^{\dagger} ), and SOAP [ 30 ] (direct on 𝑾 \bm{W} ). sections.heading: 4.3 Diffusion model personalization (Mix-of-Show)
sections.text: To test transfer beyond NLP, we evaluate AdaPreLoRA on diffusion-model personalization with the Mix-of-Show framework [ 9 ] , which uses Embedding Decomposed LoRA (EDLoRA) on the text encoder and U-Net of a Stable Diffusion backbone. Setup follows [ 37 , 9 ] with embedding tuning disabled. We report CLIP score [ 12 ] (alignment with prompt; higher is better) and FID [ 13 ] (distributional similarity to reference images; lower is better) at LoRA scaling factors 0.7 0.7 and 1.0 1.0 . Table 6 shows that AdaPreLoRA achieves the lowest FID at every scaling-optimizer combination and the best CLIP at scaling 1.0 1.0 in both SGD- and AdamW-based families, while remaining competitive with the best baseline at scaling 0.7 0.7 . This confirms that the gains from gradient-statistics-aware preconditioning carry over from text generation to image generation. Qualitative samples (Harry Potter / Hermione Granger) and per-prompt grids across LoRA scaling factors are in Appendix F .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We organized existing LoRA optimizers along two axes: (i) which invertible surrogate is used for the singular operator J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ℱ t ​ J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}\mathcal{F}_{t}J_{\mathcal{G}} , and (ii) the choice of 𝑾 \bm{W} -space preconditioner ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} (§ 2.2 , Table 1 ). This framework exposes a previously underexplored design point: pairing a non-trivial gradient-statistics-aware ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} with LoRA’s 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) \mathcal{O}((m+n)r) memory budget. We instantiate this point as AdaPreLoRA , combining an Adafactor diagonal Kronecker preconditioner ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} on 𝑾 \bm{W} with an ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} -balance criterion that selects a unique factor update from the affine solution set of ( 7 ); by construction, the resulting factor update is the closest LoRA approximation to the preconditioned 𝑾 \bm{W} -space direction under the ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} -weighted norm, and admits a closed-form expression. Across GPT-2, Mistral-7B, Qwen2-7B, and Mix-of-Show diffusion personalization, AdaPreLoRA is competitive with or improves over a representative set of LoRA optimizers while keeping peak GPU memory at the LoRA optimizer level. The two-axis framework is not specific to AdaPreLoRA: alternative choices for either axis remain open. Two natural extensions of AdaPreLoRA itself are (i) Mixture-of-Experts adapters, where each expert carries its own pair of low-rank factors and the framework applies per expert, and (ii) quantized backbones (QLoRA), where the 𝑾 \bm{W} -space gradient must be reconstructed from quantized weights and dequantization-aware preconditioner statistics. Beyond language models, extending AdaPreLoRA to diffusion transformers (DiT) requires handling the cross-attention adapters and time-conditioning structure, where the assumption that a single ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} summarizes per-step gradient statistics may need to be relaxed. We leave a systematic study of these directions to future work.

sections.text: Proposition B.1 (Computation of J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}} and J 𝒢 ∗ J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*} ) . Let [ 𝐁 , 𝐀 ] [\bm{B},\bm{A}] be a pair of low-rank factors with 𝐁 ∈ ℝ m × r , 𝐀 ∈ ℝ r × n \bm{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\bm{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} . Denote the Jacobian of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} by J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}} and its adjoint by J 𝒢 ∗ J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*} . Then, for any [ 𝐏 , 𝐐 ] ∈ [ ℝ m × r , ℝ r × n ] [\bm{P},\bm{Q}]\in[\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}] and any 𝐂 ∈ ℝ m × n \bm{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , • J 𝒢 ​ ( [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] ) ​ [ 𝑷 , 𝑸 ] = 𝑷 ​ 𝑨 + 𝑩 ​ 𝑸 J_{\mathcal{G}}([\bm{B},\bm{A}])[\bm{P},\bm{Q}]=\bm{PA}+\bm{BQ} , • J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ( [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] ) ​ ( 𝑪 ) = [ 𝑪 ​ 𝑨 ⊤ , 𝑩 ⊤ ​ 𝑪 ] J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}([\bm{B},\bm{A}])(\bm{C})=[\bm{C}\bm{A}^{\top},\bm{B}^{\top}\bm{C}] , • J 𝒢 ​ ( [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] ) ​ J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ( [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] ) ​ ( 𝑪 ) = 𝑪 ​ 𝑨 ⊤ ​ 𝑨 + 𝑩 ​ 𝑩 ⊤ ​ 𝑪 J_{\mathcal{G}}([\bm{B},\bm{A}])J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}([\bm{B},\bm{A}])(\bm{C})=\bm{C}\bm{A}^{\top}\bm{A}+\bm{B}\bm{B}^{\top}\bm{C} . • J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ( [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] ) ​ J 𝒢 ​ ( [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] ) ​ [ 𝑷 , 𝑸 ] = [ 𝑷 ​ 𝑨 ​ 𝑨 ⊤ + 𝑩 ​ 𝑸 ​ 𝑨 ⊤ , 𝑩 ⊤ ​ 𝑷 ​ 𝑨 + 𝑩 ⊤ ​ 𝑩 ​ 𝑸 ] J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}([\bm{B},\bm{A}])J_{\mathcal{G}}([\bm{B},\bm{A}])[\bm{P},\bm{Q}]=[\bm{P}\bm{A}\bm{A}^{\top}+\bm{B}\bm{Q}\bm{A}^{\top},\;\bm{B}^{\top}\bm{P}\bm{A}+\bm{B}^{\top}\bm{B}\bm{Q}] . Proof. The Jacobian operator J 𝒢 ​ ( [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] ) ​ [ 𝑷 , 𝑸 ] : [ ℝ m × r , ℝ r × n ] → ℝ m × n J_{\mathcal{G}}([\bm{B},\bm{A}])[\bm{P},\bm{Q}]:[\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} represents the derivative of 𝒢 \mathcal{G} at [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] [\bm{B},\bm{A}] along the direction [ 𝑷 , 𝑸 ] [\bm{P},\bm{Q}] . Similarly, J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ( [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] ) ​ ( 𝑪 ) : ℝ m × n → [ ℝ m × r , ℝ r × n ] J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}([\bm{B},\bm{A}])(\bm{C}):\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\rightarrow[\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}] is the adjoint of J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}} at [ 𝑩 , 𝑨 ] [\bm{B},\bm{A}] along the direction 𝑪 \bm{C} . For more details, see [ 1 , § 6.1] . (i) The computation of J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}} . sections.text: The update rule of SoLoRA is given by 𝚫 𝑨 t = ( 𝑩 t ⊤ 𝑳 t 1 2 𝑩 t ) − 1 𝑩 t ⊤ ​ 𝑮 t ⏟ 𝑮 𝑨 t 𝑹 t − 1 2 [ 𝑰 − 1 2 𝑹 t 1 2 𝑨 t ⊤ ( 𝑨 t 𝑹 t 1 2 𝑨 t ⊤ ) − 1 𝑨 t ] , 𝚫 𝑩 t = [ 𝑰 − 1 2 𝑩 t ( 𝑩 t ⊤ 𝑳 t 1 2 𝑩 t ) − 1 𝑩 t ⊤ 𝑳 t 1 2 ] 𝑳 t − 1 2 𝑮 t ​ 𝑨 t ⊤ ⏟ 𝑮 𝑩 t ( 𝑨 t 𝑹 t 1 2 𝑨 t ⊤ ) − 1 . \begin{split}\bm{\Delta}_{\bm{A}_{t}}&=(\bm{B}_{t}^{\top}\bm{L}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{B}_{t})^{-1}\underbrace{\bm{B}_{t}^{\top}\bm{G}_{t}}_{\bm{G}_{\bm{A}_{t}}}\bm{R}_{t}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\bm{I}-\frac{1}{2}\bm{R}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{A}_{t}^{\top}(\bm{A}_{t}\bm{R}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{A}_{t}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{A}_{t}}}\right],\\ \bm{\Delta}_{\bm{B}_{t}}&=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\bm{I}-\frac{1}{2}\bm{B}_{t}(\bm{B}_{t}^{\top}\bm{L}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{B}_{t})^{-1}\bm{B}_{t}^{\top}\bm{L}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}}}\right]\bm{L}_{t}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\underbrace{\bm{G}_{t}\bm{A}_{t}^{\top}}_{\bm{G}_{\bm{B}_{t}}}(\bm{A}_{t}\bm{R}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{A}_{t}^{\top})^{-1}.\end{split} We now analyze the computational complexity of computing the updates 𝚫 𝑨 t \bm{\Delta}_{\bm{A}_{t}} and 𝚫 𝑩 t \bm{\Delta}_{\bm{B}_{t}} . For simplicity, we focus on 𝚫 𝑨 t \bm{\Delta}_{\bm{A}_{t}} , as the complexity for 𝚫 𝑩 t \bm{\Delta}_{\bm{B}_{t}} is symmetric. • Compute gradient 𝑮 t \bm{G}_{t} . The stochastic gradient 𝑮 t \bm{G}_{t} of 𝑾 t \bm{W}_{t} is obtained during the backpropagation process. • Row and column sums for 𝒍 t \bm{l}_{t} and 𝒓 t \bm{r}_{t} . Compute 𝒍 t \bm{l}_{t} and 𝒓 t \bm{r}_{t} by summing the square of the element of 𝑮 t \bm{G}_{t} along rows or columns, which is in the computation 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ n ) \mathcal{O}(mn) . 𝑳 t 1 2 \bm{L}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}} and 𝑳 t − 1 2 \bm{L}_{t}^{-\frac{1}{2}} can computed in 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ) \mathcal{O}(m) , 𝑹 t 1 2 \bm{R}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}} and 𝑹 t − 1 2 \bm{R}_{t}^{-\frac{1}{2}} can computed in 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ) \mathcal{O}(n) . • Compute ( 𝑩 t ⊤ ​ 𝑳 t 1 2 ​ 𝑩 t ) − 1 ​ 𝑮 𝑨 t ​ 𝑹 t − 1 2 (\bm{B}_{t}^{\top}\bm{L}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{B}_{t})^{-1}\bm{G}_{\bm{A}_{t}}\bm{R}_{t}^{-\frac{1}{2}} . First to compute the inverse matrices ( 𝑩 t ⊤ ​ 𝑳 t 1 2 ​ 𝑩 t ) − 1 (\bm{B}_{t}^{\top}\bm{L}^{\frac{1}{2}}_{t}\bm{B}_{t})^{-1} in 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( m + r ) ​ r 2 ) \mathcal{O}((m+r)r^{2}) . Then multiply the inverse ( 𝑩 t ⊤ ​ 𝑳 t 1 2 ​ 𝑩 t ) − 1 (\bm{B}_{t}^{\top}\bm{L}^{\frac{1}{2}}_{t}\bm{B}_{t})^{-1} by 𝑮 𝑨 t \bm{G}_{\bm{A}_{t}} in 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ r 2 ) \mathcal{O}(nr^{2}) , and multiply the diagonal matrix 𝑹 t − 1 2 \bm{R}_{t}^{-\frac{1}{2}} in 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ r ) \mathcal{O}(nr) . • Compute ( 𝑩 t ⊤ ​ 𝑳 t 1 2 ​ 𝑩 t ) − 1 ​ 𝑮 𝑨 t ​ 𝑨 t ⊤ ​ ( 𝑨 t ​ 𝑹 t 1 2 ​ 𝑨 t ⊤ ) − 1 ​ 𝑨 t (\bm{B}_{t}^{\top}\bm{L}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{B}_{t})^{-1}\bm{G}_{\bm{A}_{t}}\bm{A}_{t}^{\top}(\bm{A}_{t}\bm{R}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{A}_{t}^{\top})^{-1}\bm{A}_{t} . First to compute the inverse matrices ( 𝑨 t ​ 𝑹 t 1 2 ​ 𝑨 t ⊤ ) − 1 (\bm{A}_{t}\bm{R}^{\frac{1}{2}}_{t}\bm{A}_{t}^{\top})^{-1} in 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( n + r ) ​ r 2 ) \mathcal{O}((n+r)r^{2}) . Use the result from the last step, multiply ( 𝑩 t ⊤ ​ 𝑳 t 1 2 ​ 𝑩 t ) − 1 ​ 𝑮 𝑨 t (\bm{B}_{t}^{\top}\bm{L}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{B}_{t})^{-1}\bm{G}_{\bm{A}_{t}} by 𝑨 t ⊤ \bm{A}_{t}^{\top} in computation 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ r 2 ) \mathcal{O}(nr^{2}) , then multiply ( 𝑨 t ​ 𝑹 t 1 2 ​ 𝑨 t ⊤ ) − 1 (\bm{A}_{t}\bm{R}_{t}^{\frac{1}{2}}\bm{A}_{t}^{\top})^{-1} in computation 𝒪 ⁡ ( r 3 ) \mathcal{O}(r^{3}) , and multiply 𝑨 t \bm{A}_{t} in 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ​ r 2 ) \mathcal{O}(nr^{2}) . The computation complexity of 𝚫 𝑨 t \bm{\Delta}_{\bm{A}_{t}} is 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ n + ( m + n ) ​ r 2 + r 3 ) \mathcal{O}(mn+(m+n)r^{2}+r^{3}) . The computation of 𝚫 𝑩 t \bm{\Delta}_{\bm{B}_{t}} follows a similar structure, with symmetric terms. Its complexity is also 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ n + ( m + n ) ​ r 2 + r 3 ) \mathcal{O}(mn+(m+n)r^{2}+r^{3}) . Then we have • Per Iteration Computational Complexity. Combining the computations of 𝚫 𝑨 t \bm{\Delta}_{\bm{A}_{t}} and 𝚫 𝑩 t \bm{\Delta}_{\bm{B}_{t}} , the total computation complexity per iteration is 𝒪 ⁡ ( m ​ n + ( m + n ) ​ r 2 + r 3 ) \mathcal{O}(mn+(m+n)r^{2}+r^{3}) . • Memory Complexity. The algorithm requires storing the vectors 𝒍 t \bm{l}_{t} and 𝒓 t \bm{r}_{t} in each iteration, hence the memory complexity is 𝒪 ⁡ ( m + n ) \mathcal{O}(m+n) .

sections.heading: E.1 Parameter Settings
sections.text: To ensure the reproducibility of the experiments described in Section 4 and to facilitate verification and comparison by others, we provide the complete details of the experimental parameter settings. Tables 8 and 9 list the parameters used during the fine-tuning of GPT-2 models and the learning rates corresponding to different optimizers, respectively. Specifically, we conduct experiments with GPT-2 models of various sizes. “Rank 4 (M)” represents a medium-sized model using LoRA with rank 4, while “Rank 4”, “Rank 16”, and “Rank 64” represent small models using LoRA with ranks 4, 16, and 64, respectively. To ensure the fairness of the experimental setup, we follow the parameter settings in LoRA [ 14 ] and Riemannian Preconditioned LoRA [ 37 ] . However, considering the sensitivity of different optimizers to learning rates, we use a grid search strategy to independently tune the optimal learning rate for each optimizer. This ensures that each optimizer operates under its best-performing configuration, providing more objective and reliable experimental results. We cast existing LoRA optimizers in a unified framework parameterized by two choices: (i) which invertible surrogate for J 𝒢 ∗ ​ ℱ t ​ J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}\mathcal{F}_{t}J_{\mathcal{G}} to use, and (ii) which ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} on 𝑾  m{W} to use. Existing methods occupy four families along these axes: factor-space adaptive updates, block-diagonal surrogates for J 𝒢 ∗ ​ J 𝒢 J_{\mathcal{G}}^{*}J_{\mathcal{G}} , Frobenius-residual pseudoinverse methods, and Riemannian manifold constraint. Within this design space, a gradient-statistics-aware ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} paired with a closed-form factor-space solve at 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( m + n ) ​ r ) \mathcal{O}((m+n)r) memory remains underexplored.
